facts.one_liner: Where Alpine winter tourism was born, in 1864, with a famous wager.
facts.why_go: Founded in 1856 by Johannes Badrutt, the Kulm is the hotel where, according to legend, Badrutt bet English summer guests in 1864 that they would enjoy the winter—starting Alpine winter tourism. It went on to host events of the 1928 and 1948 Winter Olympics, and the Cresta Run skeleton toboggan track still starts below the hotel. Rooms look over Lake St. Moritz to the Engadin peaks.
facts.best_time: December–March for skiing, the Cresta Run and events on the frozen lake; summer for Engadin hiking.
facts.how_to_get_there: St. Moritz station (Rhaetian Railway, including the Glacier and Bernina Express) is a short ride away; Zurich is about 3.5 hours by train.
facts.good_to_know: The hotel is seasonal; it closes in spring and autumn.

facts.one_liner: A ducal palace on the Ringstraße that became the Habsburg emperor’s guest house.
facts.why_go: Built in 1863–1865 as the Palais Württemberg and opened as a hotel for the 1873 World’s Fair, the Imperial served as Emperor Franz Joseph’s official guest house, hosting kings and statesmen. Its grand marble staircase, crystal chandeliers and the Café Imperial—home of the Imperial Torte—make it the essence of imperial Vienna, steps from the State Opera and the Musikverein.
facts.best_time: Year-round; December for Christmas markets and the ball season in January–February.
facts.how_to_get_there: Kärntner Ring 16, next to the Musikverein; Karlsplatz U-Bahn station (U1, U2, U4) is two minutes away. Vienna Airport is about 25 minutes by car or 16 minutes by CAT train.
facts.good_to_know: The Imperial Torte, created for Emperor Franz Joseph in 1873, makes a classic Viennese souvenir.

facts.one_liner: An Art Nouveau masterpiece facing the Chain Bridge and Buda Castle.
facts.why_go: Completed in 1906 for a London insurance company, the Gresham Palace is one of Budapest’s finest Art Nouveau buildings, with peacock-motif wrought-iron gates, Zsolnay ceramics and a glass-roofed arcade. After decades of decline it was restored as a Four Seasons hotel, and its Danube-view rooms look straight at the Széchenyi Chain Bridge and Buda Castle.
facts.best_time: April–June and September–October; December brings Christmas markets nearby.
facts.how_to_get_there: Széchenyi István tér 5–6, at the Pest end of the Chain Bridge; Budapest Airport is about 30 minutes by car.
facts.good_to_know: Walk across the Chain Bridge and ride the Buda Castle funicular for the classic view back over the hotel.

facts.one_liner: A cliff-top Atlantic hotel where Churchill painted and afternoon tea is a ritual.
facts.why_go: Founded by Scotsman William Reid and opened in 1891, Reid’s Palace sits on a headland above the Atlantic west of Funchal Bay, surrounded by 10 acres of subtropical gardens. Winston Churchill painted here, George Bernard Shaw took tango lessons, and its terrace afternoon tea is still Madeira’s most celebrated tradition. Saltwater pools are cut into the rocks below.
facts.best_time: Year-round—Madeira’s mild climate earns it the name “island of eternal spring”; New Year’s Eve fireworks are spectacular.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 25 minutes by car from Madeira (Cristiano Ronaldo) Airport; central Funchal is a 15-minute walk.
facts.good_to_know: Dress smartly for afternoon tea on the terrace and book ahead.

facts.why_go: Opened in 1910 at the request of King Alfonso XIII, who wanted a hotel worthy of royal guests for his wedding, the Ritz Madrid sits between the Prado Museum and the Retiro Park. After a major restoration it reopened in 2021 as the Mandarin Oriental Ritz, its listed façade gleaming and its glass-roofed Palm Court restored. facts.one_liner: The Astors’ Italianate mansion above the Thames, scene of the Profumo affair.
facts.why_go: Cliveden’s Grade I-listed mansion was built in 1851 by Charles Barry, architect of the Houses of Parliament, on a ridge 40 metres above the River Thames. Home to Nancy Astor and the famous “Cliveden Set”, it was also the setting for the 1960s Profumo affair. Today it is a hotel set in 375 acres of National Trust gardens and woodlands, with Edwardian launches cruising the river below.
facts.best_time: May–September for the gardens and river trips; autumn colours in October.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 40 minutes by car from central London and 20 minutes from Heathrow; Taplow and Burnham stations on the Elizabeth line are nearby.

facts.why_go: Opened in 1902 as the North British Station Hotel above Waverley station, The Balmoral is a Victorian landmark at the east end of Princes Street. Its 58-metre clock tower is famously set three minutes fast so travellers don’t miss their trains—except on Hogmanay. J.K. Rowling finished the last Harry Potter book in one of its suites, and many rooms look straight up to Edinburgh Castle.
facts.best_time: May–September; August for the Edinburgh festivals and late December for Hogmanay (book far ahead).
facts.how_to_get_there: 1 Princes Street, directly above Edinburgh Waverley station; Edinburgh Airport is about 25 minutes by tram or taxi.
facts.good_to_know: The Old Town’s Royal Mile is a five-minute walk across North Bridge.

facts.why_go: Built in 1926, the Biltmore’s 96-metre tower, modelled on the Giralda of Seville, made it Florida’s tallest building. Its vast pool—once the largest hotel pool in the world—employed future Tarzan star Johnny Weissmuller as a swimming instructor.
